CISA ICS Advisories.title: Siemens Building Automation and Energy Products
CISA ICS Advisories.description:
View CSAF

Summary

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project and security researchers disclosed two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime known as "php2shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines, and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Siemens is actively monitoring the situation and assessing the implications of these vulnerabilities on our portfolio. Because this evaluation is ongoing, our findings are subject to change as new technical details and vendor updates emerge. We will publish updated findings, guidance, and remediation recommendations as soon as they become available. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Building Automation and Energy Products are affected:

  • AMIS TS vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
  • blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
  • blueplanet 360 NX3 M6 WM OD IISX - S vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
  • Energy Engage V2.0SP9 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
  • Energy Engage V3.1SP1 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
  • Heliox Rapid vers:all/* ()Local Monitoring bt-monitoring-vm vers:intdot/<20261103 (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
  • Spectrum Power 3 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109619)
  • Spectrum Power 4 vers:all/*, vers:all/*, vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
  • Spectrum Power 7 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-109618
PHP uses longjmp() for out-of-memory (OOM) errors to exit the current context and abort handling of the request. Some contexts may not properly account for this scenario and leave request memory in an uninitialized state before performing an allocation. The subsequent request cleanup procedure may read or branch on this memory. Multiple OOM strategies can consistently trigger this condition and lead to remote code execution (RCE).

CVE-2026-109619
PHP has various global state that temporarily points into request memory. In some scenarios, global state may not be correctly reset, or may be repopulated after being reset. The global state may then refer to request memory even after it has been freed. Subsequent requests may read or branch on this stale state before it is fully initialized. Multiple strategies can trigger this condition and produce remote code execution (RCE).

General Recommendations

Operators of critical power systems (e.g. TSOs or DSOs) worldwide are usually required by regulations to build resilience into the power grids by applying multi-level redundant secondary protection schemes. It is therefore recommended that the operators check whether appropriate resilient protection measures are in place. The risk of cyber incidents impacting the grid's reliability can thus be minimized by virtue of the grid design. Siemens strongly recommends applying the provided security updates using the corresponding tooling and documented procedures made available with the product. If supported by the product, an automated means to apply the security updates across multiple product instances may be used. Siemens strongly recommends prior validation of any security update before being applied, and supervision by trained staff of the update process in the target environment. As a general security measure Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access with appropriate mechanisms (e.g. firewalls, segmentation, VPN). It is advised to configure the environment according to our operational guidelines in order to run the devices in a protected IT environment. Recommended security guidelines can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/gridsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Summary

Palo Alto Networks has published information on a vulnerability in PAN-OS related to the Node2Shell vulnerability. This advisory lists the related Siemens Industrial products affected by this vulnerability. Customers are advised to consult and implement the workarounds provided in Palo Alto Networks' upstream security notifications. 

The following versions of Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808 are affected:

  • RUGGEDCOM APE1808 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 9.8 Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808
1 Vulnerability
Out-of-bounds Write

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-111497
A buffer overflow vulnerability in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in Google Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. Users need to update any Brotli libraries or binaries between 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 to the latest available version: 1.0.10 or 1.1.1 or 1.2.1.
Read More

1 Affected Product

RUGGEDCOM APE1808 with Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS

CISA ICS Advisories.title: Siemens Industrial Edge Management
CISA ICS Advisories.description:
View CSAF

Summary

Siemens is currently assessing the impact of Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497) on Industrial Edge. Please check your Industrial Edge Management (IEM) setup: - No Management Applications installed: No action is required. Although the affected Brotli library is included in the IEM software stack, the affected functionality is not used or exposed. The same applies to IEDK. - Management Applications installed: Follow the specific mitigations until a fix is available. - Device Applications installed: Follow the specific mitigations until a fix is available. For Siemens-managed services, Industrial Edge Hub and Industrial Edge Management Cloud, appropriate Firewall/WAF protection has already been implemented. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens is preparing further fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Edge Management are affected:

  • Cloud Connector Configurator vers:intdot/<1.24.3 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • Common Configurator (CC on IEM) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • Common Configurator on Device (CC on Edge) vers:all/* (CVE-2026-111497)
  • Data Flow Monitoring vers:intdot/<3.0.18 (CVE-2026-111497)
  • Databus Configurator vers:intdot/<4.0.1 (CVE-2026-111497)

An OS command vulnerability exists in CoreTec product that allows authenticated users with certain roles to execute arbitrary system commands with full control over the device. CVE-2026-43284
A vulnerability exists in the IPsec ESP subsystem (esp4) of the Linux kernel used in CoreTec5 that allows a local unprivileged user to escalate privileges to root. The flaw exists in how the kernel handles memory pages when processing ESP encrypted network packets. An attacker can craft a packet that causes the kernel to decrypt data directly into memory pages it does not own, including cached copies of privileged operating system binaries. When one of those binaries is executed, the attacker's injected code runs with root privileges. In CoreTec5, the vulnerable ESP component is compiled in kernel as a built-in and is present at boot time allowing a local user to exploit it.

Product Status: known_affected

Vendor fix
Mitsubishi Electric is releasing fixed version 10.97.3 or later for GENESIS64 and ICONICS Suite. Please download the fixed version from the link below and install it: "https://iconicsinc.my.site.com/community/s/resource-center/product-downloads". (Note: GENESIS64 is included in the ICONICS Suite installation.) For more information on the fixed version, please refer to the Mitsubishi Electric security advisory at "https://www.mitsubishielectric.com/psirt/vulnerability/pdf/2026-006_en.pdf".

Mitigation
For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend configuring the PCs with the affected product installed so that only an administrator can log in, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.

Mitigation
For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend using the PCs with the affected product installed in the LAN and blocking remote login from untrusted networks and hosts, and from non-administrator users, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.

Mitigation
For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend blocking unauthorized access by using a firewall, virtual private network (VPN), etc. and allowing remote login only to administrator when internet access is required, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.

Mitigation
For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend restricting physical access to the PC with the affected product installed and the network to which the PC is connected, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.

For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend preventing the user from clicking on web links in emails from untrusted sources, or from opening attachments in untrusted emails, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.

For customers using the affected product who cannot immediately update it, Mitsubishi Electric and Mitsubishi Electric Iconics Digital Solutions recommend installing anti-virus software on the PC with the affected product installed, to minimize the risk of exploitation of this vulnerability.

Incorrect Privilege Assignment (CWE-266) vulnerability in GENESIS64, ICONICS Suite, Hyper Historian, AnalytiX, MobileHMI, and MC Works64 could allow an attacker who can log in using the same administrator account for the affected products to launch and operate DCOM objects locally or remotely. During installation, the installers of the affected products unnecessarily grant default DCOM permissions to the administrator account of the affected products. As a result, the attacker may disclose, tamper with, destroy, or delete internal information, or cause the affected system to enter a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

CISA ICS Advisories.description:
View CSAF

Summary

Successful exploitation of this these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to fully compromise the device.

The following versions of Kiloview E3 NDI Encoder are affected:

  • E3 Firmware <1.30 (CVE-2026-109122, CVE-2026-111100, CVE-2026-96616, CVE-2026-105265, CVE-2026-110491, CVE-2026-107861, CVE-2026-110243, CVE-2026-92450, CVE-2026-110825)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 9.9 Kiloview E3 Firmware
6 Vulnerabilities
Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command ('OS Command Injection'), Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Insufficient Session Expiration, Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal'), NULL Pointer Dereference, Use of Hard-coded Credentials

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Communications, Information Technology
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: China

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-109122
The network management service on affected Kiloview E3 NDI encoder firmware fails to sanitize one field used when configuring static routes via the web management API. An authenticated web user with permission to configure static routes can exploit this to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root, and the malicious configuration persists across reboots. Successful exploitation could result in full device compromise, including exposure of stored credentials and cryptographic material.

Acknowledgments

  • Juan Alonso reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:

  • Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages.
  • Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams.
  • Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

Summary

Users of Industrial Edge Devices are advised to consult the respective Security Advisories for their devices (for Siemens Industrial Edge devices see Additional Information). Industrial Edge Device Kit contains multiple path traversal vulnerabilities that could facilitate an authenticated remote attacker to access sensitive internal information. Siemens has released new versions for several affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions. Siemens recommends specific countermeasures for products where fixes are not, or not yet available.

CISA ICS Advisories.description:
View CSAF

Summary

The Industrial Edge App Publisher contains a vulnerability chain involving improper certificate validation and the rendering of unescaped data from backend responses. These issues can be combined to allow an attacker on the network to impersonate the management server and execute arbitrary code (RCE) on the local machine through Node.js integration. Siemens has released an update for the Industrial Edge App Publisher and recommends to update to the latest version.

The following versions of Siemens Industrial Edge App Publisher are affected:

  • Industrial Edge App Publisher vers:intdot/<1.27.9 (CVE-2026-78556, CVE-2026-78557)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 8.3 Siemens Industrial Edge App Publisher
2 Vulnerabilities
Improper Certificate Validation, Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-78556
The affected software does not properly validate the server certificate when initiating a TLS connection. This allows an attacker to intercept and relay communication (Man-in-the-Middle attack) and to spoof a trusted entity by interfering in the communication path between the client and the intended server.
Read More

1 Affected Product

Industrial Edge App Publisher < V1.27.9

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Vendor fix
Update to V1.27.9 or later version

View CVE Details

CVE-2026-78557
The application fails to properly sanitize or escape data received from the backend before rendering it in the user interface. Because the front end is integrated with Node.js, this vulnerability allows for the execution of arbitrary JavaScript, which can be leveraged to achieve remote code execution (RCE) on the victim's machine

CISA ICS Advisories.description:

Summary

SENTRON 3NA COM Fuse contains a Denial-of-Service vulnerability. Improper handling of a network management message could allow an attacker to trigger a denial-of-service (DoS) condition. Successful exploitation may require the affected network to be re-established to restore normal operation.

The following versions of Siemens SENTRON 3NA COM Fuse are affected:

  • SENTRON 3NA COM Fuse vers:intdot/<5.2 (CVE-2024-7322)

  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

A ZigBee coordinator, router, or end device may change their node ID when an unsolicited encrypted rejoin response is received, this change in node ID causes Denial of Service (DoS). To recover from this DoS, the network must be re-established

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA ICS Advisories.description:

Summary

PSS(R)SINCAL uses WibuKey third-party product that contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to cause a system crash, resulting in a denial-of-service condition. This affects PSS SINCAL only when configured to use the legacy WibuKey dongle license type. Siemens is actively preparing updates and recommends applicable mitigations for products where patches are currently unavailable.

The following versions of Siemens PSS(R)SINCAL are affected:

  • PSS(R)SINCAL V21.5 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-84854)
  • PSS(R)SINCAL V22.0 vers:all/* (CVE-2026-84854)
  • PSS(R)SINCAL V22.5 vers:intdot/<22.5.5 (CVE-2026-84854)

Background

  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-84854
In the WibuKey driver, insufficient validation of user input when calculating the size of a kernel buffer could cause small amounts of data to be written outside the intended kernel buffer. This can lead to a system crash. Under unfavorable circumstances, adjacent kernel memory may be modified.

CISA ICS Advisories.description:

Summary

The products listed below contain a vulnerability that could allow an attacker to boot an operating system or UEFI application signed with that test key, bypassing UEFI Secure Boot protections even when Secure Boot is enabled. Siemens has released new versions for the affected products and recommends to update to the latest versions.

The following versions of Siemens SIMATIC IPCs are affected:

  • SIMATIC IPC BX-21A vers:intdot/<31.01.13 (CVE-2026-72895)
  • SIMATIC IPC RW-543A vers:intdot/<1.1.4 (CVE-2026-72895)
  • SIMATIC IPC227G / IPC277G / IPC277G PRO / IPC327G / IPC377G vers:intdot/<28.01.15 (CVE-2026-72895)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 7.7 Siemens SIMATIC IPC BX-21A
1 Vulnerability
Use of Default Cryptographic Key

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Transportation Systems, Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Financial Services, Government Services and Facilities
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Germany

Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-72895
A BIOS vendor test key is present in the UEFI Secure Boot key database. This could allow a local attacker with physical or administrative access to the device to boot an operating system or UEFI application signed with that test key, bypassing UEFI Secure Boot protections even when Secure Boot is enabled, potentially leading to a full loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the device.
Read More

3 Affected Products

SIMATIC IPC BX-21A < V31.01.13

Product Status: known_affected

Remediations

Mitigation

Note: After upgrading to the fixed BIOS version, users must load the BIOS default settings. If Secure Boot keys were already provisioned, they must be provisioned again afterwards.

Mitigation
As a temporary mitigation, users can manually remove the test key from the database (e.g., "DO NOT TRUST - AMI Test PK" for RW-543A or "insyde-ElkhartLake" for IPC227G/277G/327G/377G and BX-21A). Note: Loading default settings will restore the test key, so upgrading remains recommended.

Vendor fix
Update to V31.01.13 or later version

Vulnerabilities

Expand All +
CVE-2026-33387
A template injection vulnerability was discovered in the Dashboards functionality due to improper validation of an input parameter. An authenticated user with the required privileges can define a dashboard containing a malicious payload, or a victim can be socially engineered into importing a malicious dashboard. When the victim views or imports the dashboard, the payload executes in their browser context, allowing the attacker to modify application data or disrupt application availability.

CVE-2026-33388
An access control vulnerability was discovered in the Credentials Manager functionality due to insufficient validation of user privileges. A remote authenticated user with limited privileges can view a limited subset of the available entries in the Credentials Manager. The actual credential values are not directly visible, but the user can delete entries or edit their properties. An attacker who deletes or edits an entry can disrupt authentication for dependent devices, and one who manipulates an entry's configuration may be able to indirectly obtain the credentials.

CVE-2026-33389
An improper certificate/host key validation vulnerability was discovered in the Smart Polling functionality, which established encrypted connections to target devices without validating the remote host's identity, and no option was provided to enable it. A man-in-the-middle attacker positioned between a sensor and a polled device can, during a polling session, impersonate the device and intercept the communication, including the credentials used to access it. The captured credentials can then be replayed to authenticate against the device itself or against other devices sharing the same credentials, allowing the attacker to access and tamper with the device's data and to disrupt its operations.

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends protecting network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends configuring the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the exploitation risk of this vulnerability.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, and ensure they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolate them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most recent version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as its connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Summary

The affected application loads dynamic-link libraries (DLLs) from an uncontrolled search path. This could allow an authenticated local attacker to place a specially crafted DLL in a directory that the application searches, leading to arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the affected application. Siemens has released a new version for Siemens Software Center and recommends to update to the latest version. Please refer to our blog post for additional information about current known active exploitation and how to detect it.

The following versions of Siemens Software Center are affected:

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Acknowledgments

  • Siemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA.

General Recommendations

As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity

Additional Resources

For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories

Terms of Use

The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

  • Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet.
  • Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.
  • When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

Summary

Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could crash the Windows kernel.

The following versions of HMS Networks PEAK-System PCAN Windows drivers are affected:

  • PEAK-System Device Driver Setup <=5.1.2.1151 (CVE-2026-109576, CVE-2026-101103, CVE-2026-94188, CVE-2026-103672, CVE-2026-110322, CVE-2026-105960)
  • PCAN Windows CAN device drivers <=5.1.2 (CVE-2026-109576, CVE-2026-101103, CVE-2026-94188, CVE-2026-103672, CVE-2026-110322, CVE-2026-105960)
CVSS Vendor Equipment
v3 7.1 HMS Networks PEAK-System Device Driver Setup
5 Vulnerabilities
Out-of-bounds Write, Buffer Copy without Checking Size of Input ('Classic Buffer Overflow'), Improper Validation of Array Index, Untrusted Pointer Dereference, Improper Handling of Length Parameter Inconsistency

Background

  • Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Transportation Systems, Healthcare and Public Health, Energy, Critical Manufacturing
  • Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide
  • Company Headquarters Location: Sweden

The parser in PEAK-System PCAN driver correctly detected the malformed record, but the loop iterating the record list advanced its processed-bytes counter even when a record had been rejected as invalid.

Recommended Practices

CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as virtual private networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. These vulnerabilities are not exploitable remotely.

Advisory at a Glance

Title #StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware
Original Publication  October 20, 2026
Executive Summary

This advisory details recent activity by the SafePay ransomware group. SafePay actors have been highly active since August 2024, targeting businesses and critical infrastructure across North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay actors typically gain access to networks by stealing or guessing passwords, exploiting vulnerabilities in security systems, and using phishing tactics. 

Once inside the network, SafePay actors establish control by creating new accounts or taking over existing ones. They then use legitimate system tools to move through the network, identify valuable files, and disable security protections to avoid detection. Next, they encrypt the victim’s files, making them inaccessible, and leave a ransom note demanding payment in cryptocurrency. This advisory urges organizations to follow recommended security measures to reduce the risk and impact of SafePay ransomware attacks.
Affected Products
  • CVE-2020-3259 [Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor]
  • CVE-2023-20269 [CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel]
  • CVE-2023-27532 [CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function]
  • CVE-2024-40711 [CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data]
  • CVE-2024-40766 [CWE-284: Improper Access Control]
Key Actions
  • Regularly patch and update systems, especially firewalls, and other edge devices.
  • Implement Zero Trust Principle.
  • Restrict administrative tools and privileges to necessary users only.
  • Strengthen account security by implementing identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies and multifactor authentication (MFA).
Indicators of Compromise

For a downloadable copy of indicators of compromise, see: 

  • AA26-293A STIX XML (40 KB)
  • AA26-293A STIX JSON (38 KB)
Intended Audience

Organizations: Government; Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB); State, Local, Tribal, and Territorial (SLTT); Critical Infrastructure

Roles: Defensive cybersecurity analysts, vulnerability analysts, security systems managers, and operational technology (OT) owners and operators

Introduction

Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources. 

The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), United States Secret Service (USSS), Germany’s Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency, and the United Kingdom’s North West Regional Organised Crime Unit—hereafter referred to as the authoring agencies—are releasing this joint advisory to disseminate known SafePay ransomware TTPs and IOCs identified through FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations as recently as August 2026.

Since August 2024, SafePay ransomware group’s operations have affected a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia. SafePay ransomware was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026. The SafePay threat actors have impacted at least 600 separate victims from multiple critical infrastructure sectors.

The authoring agencies encourage organizations to implement the recommendations in the Mitigations section of this advisory to reduce the likelihood and impact of SafePay ransomware incidents.

Download the PDF version of this report:

#StopRansomware: SafePay Ransomware (PDF, 1.06 MB )

For a downloadable copy of IOCs, see:

AA26-293A-STIX XML (XML, 40.23 KB )
AA26-293A-STIX JSON (JSON, 37.49 KB )

Technical Details

Note: This advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK® Matrix for Enterprise framework, version 20. See MITRE ATT&CK Tactics and Techniques section of this advisory for a table of the threat actors’ activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics and techniques.

Initial Access

The FBI, USSS, and cybersecurity researchers observed SafePay threat actors obtaining initial access [TA0001] to organizations through various means, including credential exposure, implementing brute force password attacks [T1110], and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access. SafePay threat actors use the IP addresses of the VPN provider “Mullvad” to attain initial access—specifically, SafePay threat actors use phished account profiles to access victim networks to exploit the following known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) for edge device products:

  • CVE-2020-3259 [Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor]
  • CVE-2023-20269 [CWE-288: Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel] 

Additionally, the authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors exploiting the following vulnerabilities across internet-exposed systems [T1190] for initial access through automated scripts:

  • CVE-2023-27532 [CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function]
  • CVE-2024-40711 [CWE-502: Deserialization of Untrusted Data]
  • CVE-2024-40766 [CWE-284: Improper Access Control]

Execution, Persistence, Stealth, and Defense Impairment

After SafePay threat actors gain access to a victim network, they establish persistence by gaining administrative privileges on existing accounts [T1098], or on newly created accounts [T1136], using built-in administrative tools consistent with living off the land (LOTL) techniques. Once SafePay threat actors establish a foothold in a victim’s network, they use LOTL binaries (LOLBins) [T1218], such as PsExec [T1021.002] and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) [T1021.006], to execute commands on remote systems. In several instances, SafePay threat actors used ShareFinder.ps1—a PowerShell script function used for enumerating network file shares in Windows Active Directory environments—to identify valuable assets for exfiltration [T1059.001, T1059.003]. Additionally, SafePay threat actors used SharpShares.exe, a tool used to identify and enumerate network file shares.

As SafePay threat actors prepare for lateral movement, they commonly disable security software [T1685] to avoid detection. In some cases, the threat actors changed the passwords of system users, making valid logins impossible. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code [T1027.002].

Privilege Escalation

The authoring agencies observed SafePay threat actors using a User Account Control (UAC) Bypass Privilege Escalation technique [T1548.002] that creates an elevated process through a specified component object model, enabling the execution of malicious commands or binaries [T1059]. SafePay threat actors have also been observed using token impersonation methods [T1134.001].

Lateral Movement

To pivot laterally through a network and identify files for exfiltration [TA0010] and encryption, SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools like PsExec, WinRM, and Remote Management and Monitoring [T1569.002] software. They also employ Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) [T1021.001, T1133] to expand their presence within the compromised network [T1021]. As SafePay threat actors move laterally through a network, they look for credentials to gain admin access and will create accounts, if needed.

Collection, Exfiltration, and Impact

SafePay threat actors use legitimate tools, such as FileZilla, 7-Zip, RClone, and WinRAR to compress files and collect data [T1560.001], and WinSCP and RClone to facilitate the exfiltration of data [T1048] from the compromised network to actor-controlled accounts. In some instances, SafePay threat actors use OneDrive to exfiltrate data [T1567]. In other instances, the SafePay threat actors installed legitimate remote desktop tools like AnyDesk or TeamViewer on the victim’s systems. SafePay threat actors use these tools to transfer ransomware and other software onto a victim’s system. Additionally, SafePay threat actors halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset Network Attached Storage containing victim backup data to initial factory settings to inhibit system recovery attempts [T1490].

Following exfiltration, SafePay threat actors encrypt files [T1486] using a sophisticated hybrid encryption scheme to lock data. This involves combining a ChaCha20 stream cipher with an RSA public-key cryptosystem for a fast and secure key exchange. This multilayered approach customizes encryption methods based on file type and size and enables full or partial encryption. Data encrypted with the SafePay ransomware variant (appended with .SafePay) cannot be recovered without the decryption key. SafePay threat actors hold the encrypted data for ransom and typically demand a subset of company revenue in cryptocurrency in exchange for decryption software. SafePay threat actors leave a ransom note on the victim’s system, typically on the desktop or root directory, advising them that SafePay locked their system and to reach out over a chat portal at a TOR .onion website link with a victim ID as the login. To put pressure on the victim, a representative makes phone calls on behalf of the ransomware group. If the victim does not pay, SafePay posts the exfiltrated data to their SafePay leak website, which is linked in the ransom note. Following encryption, SafePay may delete itself from the victim’s filesystem [T1070.004].

Leveraged Tools

Table 1 lists publicly available tools and applications used by SafePay threat actors, including legitimate tools repurposed for their operations.
Note: These tools and applications should not be attributed as malicious without analytical evidence to support threat actor use and/or control.

Table 1. Tools Leveraged by SafePay Threat Actors
Tool Name Description
7-Zip An open source software that enables users to compress various file formats. SafePay threat actors maliciously use 7-Zip for data packaging and movement.
FileZilla An open source client that enables users to transfer files between servers. SafePay threat actors use FileZilla maliciously for data exfiltration.
Mimikatz A credential dumper that enables users to view and save authentication credentials, such as Kerberos tickets [T1550.002]. SafePay threat actors use Mimikatz for password exfiltration.
PowerShell A cross-platform task automation solution used for various malicious activities, including command execution. It is composed of a command-line shell, a scripting language, and a configuration management framework—which runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS. 
PsExec A tool designed to run programs that SafePay threat actors use to execute commands on remote systems.
RClone A legitimate command-line program used to sync files with cloud storage services, such as Mega. SafePay threat actors maliciously use RClone for data packaging and movement.
ScreenConnect A remote support, access, and meeting software that allows users to control devices remotely over the internet. SafePay threat actors use ScreenConnect for persistence and access.
ShareFinder.ps1 A PowerShell script used to scan an Active Directory network for shared folders. SafePay threat actors use ShareFinder.ps1 for exfiltration hunting.
WinRAR Archive utility used to split compromised data into segments and to compress [T1560.001] files into a .RAR format prior to exfiltration. SafePay threat actors use WinRAR for data packaging and movement.
WinRM A Windows-based protocol designed to facilitate remote management and automation. SafePay threat actors use WinRM for command execution.
AnyDesk and TeamViewer Legitimate remote desktop tool used for accessing and controlling computers over the internet. SafePay threat actors use AnyDesk and TeamViewer to transfer malware to the victim’s system.
AcronisDiskDirector A legitimate disk management tool.
SharpShares.exe A network scanning tool used for host discovery and enumeration.
NetExec A legitimate network assessment tool to enumerate systems, validate credentials, and manage remote operations across private networks.
Backblaze A command-line tool for file management within Backblaze B2 cloud storage. SafePay threat actors executed commands via b2.exe to exfiltrate a victim’s data.

Technique Title ID Use
Data Encrypted for Impact  T1486 SafePay threat actors encrypt data on targeted systems to disrupt access to a particular system or network service. They then demand a ransom payment in exchange for a decryption key.
Inhibit System Recovery  T1490 SafePay threat actors disable services designed to assist in recovery of a corrupted system. In some cases, SafePay threat actors deleted all network-attached backups of company data.

Incident Response

If a potential compromise is detected, but ransomware actors have not (yet) encrypted items, organizations should take the following actions:

  1. Determine which hosts were compromised and isolate them by quarantining or taking them offline.
  2. Initiate threat hunting activities to scope the intrusion. Collect and review relevant artifacts, logs, and other data to identify threat actor TTPs, compromised devices and accounts, a timeline of activity, etc.
  3. Report the suspected compromise to the FBI and other agencies as appropriate (if located within the U.K., report the compromise to Report Fraud or local police force) (see the Reporting section for contact information).
  4. Apply eviction countermeasures, including those listed below, to contain the incident and eradicate the threat actor from the network (Note: Start applying countermeasures after collecting enough threat hunting data to inform effective countermeasure selection; this will likely overlap with threat hunting activities). 
    1. Use CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool to assemble countermeasures for a systematic eviction plan—the tool comprises Playbook-NG (a web application) and COUN7ER (a database of post-compromise countermeasures mapped to adversary TTPs). 
      1. Use Playbook-NG and COUN7ER together to assemble a systematic eviction plan, or playbook, that leverages distinct countermeasures to contain and evict cyber threat actors. The playbook features a list of recommended response actions based on threat actor TTPs and includes each action’s intended outcome, preparatory steps, and associated risks. For more information, see CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool fact sheet.
  5. Harden the network to prevent additional malicious activity (see Mitigations for guidance).

If compromise is detected and items have been encrypted, see the “Ransomware and Data Extortion Response Checklist” in CISA’s joint #StopRansomware Guide.

Mitigations

The authoring agencies recommend organizations implement the mitigations below to improve their cybersecurity posture on the basis of the threat actors’ activity. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement. CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures. Visit CISA’s CPGs webpage for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections.

Organizations should implement the following mitigations:

  • Prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities (KEVs) and keep all operating systems, software, and firmware up to date, as timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats; specifically, prioritize patching KEVs in internet-facing systems. [CPG 2.B].
    • Additionally, using Binding Operational Directive 26-04 offers a framework for patch prioritization based on technology type and steps for forensics triage. Under its implementation guidance, it offers guidance and steps to perform forensic triage for severe vulnerability cases.
  • Implement identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies across the organization and require MFA for all services to the greatest extent possible—particularly for webmail, VPNs, and accounts that access critical systems [CPG 3.F].
  • Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service accounts, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to comply with NIST’s digital identity guidelines; require employees to use long passwords and consider not requiring recurring password changes, as these can weaken security [CPG 3.B].
    • Use longer passwords consisting of at least 15 characters and no more than 64 characters in length.
    • Store passwords in a hashed format using industry-recognized password managers.
    • Add password user “salts” to shared login credentials.
    • Avoid reusing passwords [CPG 3.C].
    • Implement multiple failed login attempt account lockouts [CPG 3.E].
    • Disable password “hints.”
    • Refrain from requiring password changes more frequently than once per year.
      Note: NIST guidance suggests favoring longer passwords instead of requiring frequent password resets. Frequent password resets are more likely to result in users developing password patterns cyber threat actors can easily decipher.
  • Maintain offline backups of data and regularly test and maintain backup and restoration processes [CPG 3.O]; implementing this practice helps organizations avoid severe operational interruptions and prevents scenarios in which data is irretrievable.
  • Ensure all backup data is encrypted, immutable (i.e., cannot be altered or deleted), and covers the entire organization’s data infrastructure [CPG 3.K].
  • Implement a recovery plan to maintain and retain multiple copies of sensitive or proprietary data and servers in a physically separate, segmented, and secure location (e.g., hard drives, storage devices, or the cloud) [CPG 3.I, 3.O, 1.C].
  • Segment networks to prevent the spread of ransomware, as network segmentation can help control traffic flows between, and access to, various subnetworks and restrict adversary lateral movement [CPG 3.I].
  • Identify, detect, and investigate abnormal activity and potential traversal of the indicated ransomware with a network monitoring tool [CPG 4.B].
    • To aid in detecting ransomware, implement a tool that logs and reports all network traffic, including lateral movement activity on a network.
    • Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tools are particularly useful for detecting lateral connections as they have insight into common and uncommon network connections for each host.
  • Filter network traffic by preventing unknown or untrusted origins from accessing remote services on internal systems—this prevents threat actors from directly connecting to remote access services that they have established for persistence.
  • Review domain controllers, servers, workstations, and Active Directories for new, unactive and/or unrecognized accounts.
  • Disable unused ports.
  • Consider adding an email banner to emails received from outside of your organization. 
  • Audit user accounts with administrative privileges and configure access controls according to the principle of least privilege [CPG 3.G].
  • Implement time-based access for accounts set at the admin level and higher; for example, the Just-in-Time (JIT) access method provisions privileged access when needed and can support enforcement of the principle of least privilege (as well as the Zero Trust Maturity Model).
    • This is a process where a network-wide policy is set in place to automatically disable admin accounts at the Active Directory level when the account is not in direct need.
    • Individual users may submit their requests through an automated process that grants them access to a specified system for a set timeframe when they need to support the completion of a certain task.
  • Disable command-line and scripting activities and permissions, since privilege escalation and lateral movement often depend on software utilities running from the command line; if threat actors cannot run these tools, they will have difficulty escalating privileges and moving laterally [CPG 3.M].

These mitigations align with principles provided in the joint guide Shifting the Balance of Cybersecurity Risk: Principles and Approaches for Secure by Design Software. CISA urges software manufacturers to take ownership of improving the security outcomes of their customers by applying these and other secure by design tactics. By implementing secure by design tactics, software manufacturers can make their product lines secure “out of the box” without requiring customers to make additional configuration changes, purchasing product security add-in software and logs, monitoring, and making frequent security updates.

Validate Security Controls

In addition to applying mitigations, the authoring agencies recommend exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory.

To get started:

  1. Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 6 to Table 16).
  2. Align your security technologies against the technique.
  3. Test your technologies against the technique.
  4. Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance.
  5. Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data.
  6. Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process.

The authoring agencies recommend continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory.

Resources

  • Stopransomware.gov is a whole-of-government approach that provides one central location for ransomware resources and alerts.
  • CISA’s #StopRansomware Guide provides organizations with comprehensive best practices to mitigate the risk of ransomware attacks.
  • CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog is an authoritative resource for organizations to support improvement of their patch management best practices.
  • CISA’s Multifactor Authentication webpage provides best practices for network defenders to mitigate threats to accounts and systems that use MFA.
  • CISA’s Cyber Hygiene Services help organizations reduce the risk of a successful cyberattack.
  • USSS’s Preparing for a Cyber Incident outlines basic steps an organization can take before, during, and after a cyber incident.
  • CISA’s Cyber Security Evaluation Tool (CSET) provides a systematic, disciplined, and repeatable approach for evaluating an organization’s security posture; see Downloading and Installing CSET for step-by-step guidance to help your organization evaluate cybersecurity practices on your networks.
  • CISA’s Ransomware Risk Assessment helps assess an organization’s ability to counteract a ransomware infection.
  • Department of Health and Human Services’ Cybersecurity Performance Goals is a resource to help healthcare organizations implement high-impact cybersecurity practices.
  • CISA’s Binding Operational Directive 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and its implementation guidance 
  • CISA’s CI Fortify: Strengthening Resilience Across Critical Infrastructure
  • CISA’s Eviction Strategies Tool enables incident response teams to quickly turn observed behaviors into remediation plans
  • U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre 
  • U.K.’s National Crime Agency 

Reporting

Your organization has no obligation to respond or provide information to the FBI and other authoring agencies in response to this joint advisory. If, after reviewing the information provided, your organization decides to provide information to the FBI or other authoring agencies, reporting must be consistent with applicable state and federal laws.

The FBI and other authoring agencies are interested in any information, to include boundary logs showing communication to and from foreign IP addresses, a sample ransom note, communications with threat actors, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files, and/or a benign sample of an encrypted file.

Additional details of interest include a targeted company point of contact, status and scope of infection, estimated loss, operational impact, transaction IDs, date of infection, date detected, initial attack vector, and host- and network-based indicators.

The authoring agencies do not encourage paying ransom as payment does not guarantee victim files will be recovered. Furthermore, payment may also embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or fund illicit activities. Regardless of whether you or your organization have decided to pay the ransom, the FBI and CISA urge you to promptly report ransomware incidents to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3), a local FBI field office, a local USSS Field Office, or CISA via the agency’s Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center (contact@cisa.dhs.gov) or by calling 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472).

In the U.K., report incidents of a cybercrime or fraud at the UK’s Home for Reporting Cyber Crime & Fraud or 0300-123-2040, your local police force, or use the non-emergency number 101.

As a result, an address associated with malicious activity at one point in time may later be reassigned to benign services.
